For this reason he wrongly contrasts the reality actually known by human beings with some “true” reality—the “thing in itself”—that supposedly remains inaccessible to cognition.
What we know, on this account, is not that “true” reality itself, but a product arising from the interaction between it and the consciousness that knows it: a “phenomenon.”
Truth therefore ceases to mean reality itself revealing itself through human consciousness and our knowledge of reality. Instead, truth becomes knowledge itself, possessing a certain content.
Kant himself understands this content as the product of an interaction between consciousness and a reality that, in its pure form, cannot be known.

But because the nature of this interaction remains obscure, and because we cannot separate what comes from reality from what depends only on consciousness, the criterion of truth can no longer be found by empirically comparing knowledge with reality. It has to be sought, in a purely rationalist way, through an examination—or “critique”—of knowledge itself.

It is hardly surprising that Kant’s immediate successors, especially Fichte, discarded what seemed to them an unnecessary concept: the concept of reality, or the “thing in itself.” The result was pure idealism.

The source of the whole problem is easy to see. It lies in separating form from content and treating cognition as an instrument fundamentally different from, and independent of, the material on which it operates.
If cognition is an instrument made of something different from reality, then using it must indeed distort reality.
And if reality exists entirely without knowledge, then there is nothing surprising about its being inaccessible to knowledge.
So if we retain a realist concept of reality, we are driven toward a sceptical or agnostic rejection of truth, and therefore toward a denial of knowledge.
If, on the other hand, we want to preserve the idea of true knowledge, we are driven toward an idealist denial of reality and a rationalist search for the criterion of truth within knowledge itself.
But we have already seen that examining knowledge by itself gives us no way to distinguish true knowledge from false knowledge. So this route also ends, in practice, in scepticism.

If Phenomenology understood its object in the same way Kant did—if it studied knowledge independently of reality—it could hardly achieve its purpose. Instead of preparing the way for true knowledge, it would demonstrate that true knowledge is impossible.
Hegelian Phenomenology understands its object quite differently.
It begins from a genuinely realist—or “materialist”—conception of truth as reality revealing itself to itself through human consciousness, cognition, and knowledge.

It knows that rationalist attempts to find the criterion of truth within knowledge alone are just as hopeless as empiricist attempts to compare the content of consciousness with reality while remaining entirely inside consciousness.

Phenomenology therefore turns toward what we might call experimentalism. It finds the criterion of truth in technical verification through work and revolutionary verification through struggle—tests that take place in reality itself.

The products of these “techniques”—work and revolution—combine knowledge and reality so closely that the two become virtually inseparable. An airplane or a State, for example, can equally well be understood as a product of knowledge about reality or as the realization of knowledge in reality.
Phenomenology therefore understands that knowledge cannot be separated from reality and studied independently of it.

If truth is reality revealing itself through knowledge, and if Phenomenology aims to prepare the possibility of true knowledge, then Phenomenology cannot study some vague “consciousness in general,” some cognition or knowledge “as such” existing nowhere in particular and made of no one knows what.
It must study real knowledge that reveals reality itself through its meaningful content.
We can now see that Phenomenology arrives at the definition of its object directly from the goal it has set itself.
It wants to prepare philosophical knowledge: concrete knowledge, or knowledge of concrete reality.
Reality “in general” may of course exist without human beings knowing it. But once human beings exist and actually speak about reality, concrete reality genuinely includes this speech about itself.
Concrete reality is therefore inseparable from concrete knowledge, and concrete knowledge is likewise inseparable from reality.
What concretely exists is reality revealed in knowledge—or, what amounts to the same thing, knowledge revealing reality.
And because Phenomenology studies concrete knowledge, it must study precisely this kind of knowledge, not some abstraction called “knowledge in general.”

For Phenomenology, then, knowledge and cognition are not instruments that somehow exist outside reality and independently of it and are then applied to reality from outside, with no explanation of where they came from.
If they are indeed instruments that reveal reality, they are nevertheless real instruments, forged by reality itself and, so to speak, for its own use.
They therefore cannot distort reality simply by being applied to it.

If we like, we can say that the instrument of cognition changes reality when applied to it, just as any instrument changes the material on which it works. But these changes must not be treated as distortions.
The instrument, its use, and the changes produced by that use are just as real as the supposedly “untouched” reality that existed beforehand.

Indeed, only reality as modified through cognition exists concretely and actually. “Untouched” reality is itself merely an abstraction or fiction, just as unreal as an instrument of knowledge imagined apart from the reality to which it is applied.

From the standpoint of “naive” realism—the standpoint of rationalists and empiricists, and one shared more or less consciously by all the “sciences” in the narrower sense—cognition can be compared to the scaffolding used to construct a building.
Once the building is finished, the scaffolding is removed, and the building itself—the “true” reality—would supposedly stand revealed to the observer.
But to what observer? That remains a mystery.
First, this building could not be revealed to human beings without knowledge, because reality without cognition would remain inaccessible to them.

Second, even if we imagined some “divine” observer contemplating the building after the scaffolding had been removed, what this observer saw would not be reality itself. It would merely be an abstraction that exists as such only in human consciousness.
Rationalism—and idealism—makes the opposite mistake. It imagines that if we abstract from reality, we can discover “true” consciousness and knowledge in their “pure form.”
Phenomenology knows instead that knowledge is nothing other than the revelation of reality.
Remove reality, and nothing remains to be revealed. What remains is therefore nothing.
By proceeding in this way we reveal nothing at all, and knowledge itself collapses into nothingness.
From the standpoint of Phenomenology, then, knowledge and reality are inseparable.
Phenomenology can therefore study not knowledge “in itself,” but knowledge that reveals reality. Yet if it does so, it necessarily also deals with reality as revealed in and through knowledge.
Even so, its theme remains the study of knowledge, not reality. Knowledge, rather than reality, is its object.

Reality revealing itself in knowledge, on the one hand, and knowledge revealing reality, on the other, are two inseparable and complementary aspects of one and the same thing: known reality or realized knowledge—that is, truth.
Knowledge and reality form an inseparable whole, like the red and green sides of the same apple.
Yet we can look at an apple from either side, and it is equally correct to say that it is red on one side and green on the other.
The same is true of truth.
We can regard truth either as reality revealed in knowledge or as knowledge that reveals reality.
Phenomenology takes it in the second sense.
So despite everything, Phenomenology is not a discourse on reality—an onto-logy or “metaphysics.” It is a discourse on knowledge—a gnoseo-logy, a theory of cognition.
But it is a discourse on concrete, and therefore philosophical, knowledge: a philosophical or concrete theory of cognition.
In truth itself, the ontological and gnoseological—or logical—aspects of discourse coincide completely.

For this reason, in the systematic exposition of truth—that is, in systematic Philosophy—a discourse on reality, or Ontology, is inseparable from a discourse on knowledge, or Gnoseology; and both are inseparable from a discourse on the “concept,” that is, Logic.
Phenomenology, however, does not yet deal with truth itself. Its task is to prepare the possibility of true knowledge.
Put very briefly, it deals not with true knowledge but with “false” knowledge.
And false knowledge that reveals reality does not coincide with the reality revealed within that consciousness.
Phenomenology can therefore separate these two aspects and legitimately study only one of them.
Yet although Phenomenology restricts itself to the study of knowledge, it does not study “consciousness in general,” cognition “as such,” knowledge “in itself,” or some kind of “pure” knowledge.
It studies consciousness, cognition, and knowledge of reality.
For this reason, it may sometimes seem that Phenomenology is speaking about reality from beginning to end.
But what appears there is not reality itself. It is only reality as reflected in “false” knowledge—that is, reality as the content of this knowledge.
Of course, even false knowledge is real in the sense that it actually occurs within reality. It therefore reveals reality in some way.
And we will see that such knowledge is “false” only because it presents itself as universal or complete while in fact remaining one-sided.
If we examine false knowledge, we can isolate the aspect of reality that it does reveal. If we then combine all these aspects, we obtain full or true knowledge of reality.
But carrying out that analysis of the reality revealed through cognition is simply not the task of Phenomenology itself.
Thus, although Phenomenology studies only knowledge, it does not separate the “form” of knowledge from its “content.” It studies knowledge of reality.
And the reality embraced by Phenomenology in the fullest sense is concrete reality.
What exists concretely is not “reality in general,” but the real material world: the natural world of mountains, rivers, and forests, as well as the technical world of houses, roads, and cars.
And this real world genuinely includes the real subject who knows it, together with that subject’s historical, social, and political world.
So when Phenomenology studies knowledge of concrete reality, it studies knowledge of both the natural and the human world.
Let us say it once more: it studies knowledge of this real world, not the world itself in its reality.
But knowledge of this world is itself real, and Phenomenology studies not only knowledge of concrete reality but also the concrete reality of knowledge.
Real, concrete knowledge exists in the real world in the person of human beings.
Phenomenology therefore studies not “consciousness in general” or some kind of “world-reason,” but human consciousness and human reason.

In other words, it studies concrete human knowledge of the concrete world. It studies not the world in its reality, but the world as it is revealed or manifested to human beings—that is, if we like, the appearance of the world to humanity, its phenomenon.
This is where the name comes from: phenomeno-logy, a discourse or science of appearance and appearances.
Now, the real world includes humanity itself.
So when the world “manifests” itself to human beings, the world is in one sense appearing to itself.
Phenomenology therefore studies not only the ways in which the world appears to human beings, but also the ways in which human beings appear to themselves.
It studies not reality itself but knowledge of reality. And this concrete knowledge is itself nothing other than a human being.
So the “appearance” of the world reveals not so much the world as the human being to whom that world appears.
In this sense, Phenomenology can be described not as a discourse or science of the world—not as a cosmo-logy—but as a discourse or science of human beings: an anthropology.
Yet it studies human beings not simply in their reality, but insofar as they manifest themselves within the world—insofar as they are a “phenomenon.”
The object of Phenomenology is therefore not simply the human being, but the appearance of the human being to the human being.
So although we can call Phenomenology an anthropology, we must now add that it is a phenomenological anthropology.

Since for human beings the appearance of humanity to itself amounts to an experience of oneself—to becoming aware of oneself or becoming self-conscious—we can define Phenomenology still more precisely as the science of human self-consciousness.
And because self-consciousness reveals to human beings a human being within the world, Phenomenology studies not only the appearances of humanity to itself, but also appearances of the world.
It is therefore phenomenology in the full sense of the word.
And because the experience of oneself involves both cognition and knowledge, Phenomenology, in studying self-consciousness, studies both and is therefore also a gnoseology.

At the same time, because it does not separate form from content, and because the content of self-consciousness is knowledge of humanity, it is also—while remaining a gnoseology—a phenomenological anthropology.
So we can call it, with equal justification, a phenomenological gnoseology, a phenomenological anthropology, an anthropological gnoseology, or a gnoseological anthropology.
But Phenomenology does not study human cognition and “appearances” simply out of curiosity. Its specific purpose is to make true knowledge possible.
Self-consciousness interests it only insofar as self-consciousness contains this knowledge, or the real possibility from which Phenomenology itself can arise.
And we know that the only criterion of the truth of knowledge is technical and revolutionary verification.
But revolutionary verification takes place in time. It marks the transition from one form of knowledge, consciousness, and self-consciousness to another.
Phenomenology therefore studies the appearance of human beings to themselves not only at some particular moment, but throughout its temporal—that is, historical—development.
In other words, it studies the becoming, evolution, development, or history of the way human beings—and the world—appear to human beings.
